title: Forests Eat Their Own Leaves 🍂
title_options: Fallen Leaves Partly Turn Into Air 🍂
seo_intro:
Where do fallen leaves go? They get eaten by the forest: fungi, earthworms, mites, springtails and bacteria break them down.
Much of each leaf's carbon returns to the air as carbon dioxide, and the rest becomes soil that feeds the trees, so the forest recycles its own leaves.
sources_text: soil-ecology research on leaf-litter decomposition (fungi as the main decomposers; in a French beech forest, mineralization to CO2 was the main pathway, Ngao et al. 2005; the share varies between forests); Minnesota Forest Resources Council, "Earthworms invade our forest floor" (2016), on nightcrawlers pulling leaves into their burrows; Charles Darwin, The Formation of Vegetable Mould through the Action of Worms (1881)
sources: Minnesota Forest Resources Council, Earthworms invade our forest floor (2016) — https://fmr.org/news/2016/09/18/earthworms-invade-our-forest-floor
Rubino et al. (2007), isotopic method for litter carbon fluxes: part of litter carbon stays in soil instead of being respired — https://eprints.keele.ac.uk/4826/
Ngao et al. (2005), French beech forest: mineralization (CO2) was the main pathway of litter decomposition (cited in litter-carbon reviews)
Charles Darwin (1881), The Formation of Vegetable Mould through the Action of Worms

tiktok_text:
Where do fallen leaves go? 🍂 They get eaten. Fungi spread white threads through each leaf, earthworms drag leaves into their burrows at night, mites and springtails shred the rest and bacteria finish the job. Much of the leaves' carbon goes back into the air as CO₂, and the rest becomes soil that feeds the trees.

Which surprised you most: the worms, the fungi or the air? 👇
